passage: Long ago, some stories came out in a magazine one part at a time. Each part ended at an exciting moment, such as a rider falling from a horse. Some readers today think the writers loved these cliffhangers and built their books around them. But the writers' own papers tell a different story. Later, when the parts no longer had to sell magazines, the same stories were printed as whole books. The writers took the cliffhangers out, and the rider now got home safely. One writer even asked his publisher if he could skip "the usual cliffhanger" in a quiet part. The publisher said no. For these writers, the exciting endings were a matter of ______.
prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
key_logic: The writers took the cliffhangers out once "the parts no longer had to sell magazines," and one who asked to skip "the usual cliffhanger" was told no, so the endings were something required of them: a matter of obligation.

distractor_map.role: unthinking routine; ruled out because a writer asked permission to skip the cliffhanger
the critics' reading (the writers built their books around it); ruled out because they removed it as soon as they could
accident; ruled out because the break was "the usual" one and was discussed with the publisher

changes: passage cut from 127 to 115 words
'critics now read the device as architecture' turned into 'Some readers today think the writers loved these cliffhangers and built their books around them'
'the usual precipice' reworded as 'the usual cliffhanger'; 'suspended action' and 'suspended ending' reworded as 'exciting moment' and 'exciting endings'
'ran parts together and smoothed the joins' simplified to 'took the cliffhangers out'
clause 'the same letter discusses where a scene should end in quite different terms' cut (it only reinforced the ruling-out of chance/habit)
stem reworded from 'most logical and precise word or phrase' to 'Which word best completes the sentence?'
key word obligation kept; all three distractor words kept

passage: In soccer, goalkeepers dive left or right on almost every penalty kick. Yet many kicks go straight down the middle, so standing still would stop more of them. Some experts say keepers just hate the feeling of doing nothing. Keepers explain it in a narrower way. If a keeper dives and the ball goes in, people say a good kicker fooled him. If he stands still and the ball goes in, people say he failed to move. The goal counts the same either way. So choosing between the two is really a choice about ______.
prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
key_logic: Both ways of losing give up the same goal and differ only in what people say afterward ("a good kicker fooled him" versus "he failed to move"), so the choice is about blame.

distractor_map.role: the rival the first sentences set up (standing still would stop more kicks), which keepers override rather than act on
visible in the dive but does not tell the two outcomes apart, since the goal counts the same
the experts' 'hate doing nothing' explanation, not the keepers' own reason

changes: passage rewritten at grade 5 (81 words in source; 94 here, added "In soccer" framing)
'ninety-four percent of penalty kicks' simplified to 'almost every penalty kick'
'Economists call this action bias and put it down to the discomfort of doing nothing' simplified to 'Some experts say keepers just hate the feeling of doing nothing'
'outguessed by a good striker' reworded as 'a good kicker fooled him'; 'failed to react' as 'failed to move'
stem reworded to 'Which word best completes the sentence?'
key word blame kept; all three distractor words kept

passage: Seismometers are machines that record shaking in the ground. All over the world, they pick up a steady hum. The hum is made by ocean waves pushing on the sea floor. Networks built to find earthquakes remove the hum before they look for anything else, because a small quake can be lost beneath it. Then scientists found a new use for the hum. By comparing it at two faraway stations, they could study the rock in between, just as they would with an earthquake, but without waiting for one. On the earthquake networks, though, the hum was, and still is, ______.
prompt: Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?
key_logic: The earthquake networks "remove the hum before they look for anything else, because a small quake can be lost beneath it," which is how they treat noise.

distractor_map.role: something used to measure; ruled out because the earthquake networks remove the hum before looking at anything
a departure from the normal; ruled out by 'a steady hum' picked up 'all over the world'
a fault in the machine; ruled out by 'made by ocean waves pushing on the sea floor'

changes: passage rewritten at grade 6 (91 words in source; 100 here, added a one-clause gloss of seismometers)
'periods of five to twenty seconds' cut
'correlate the hum recorded at pairs of distant stations' simplified to 'comparing it at two faraway stations'
'measured the structure of the crust' simplified to 'study the rock in between'
distractor 'an instrument' replaced by 'a tool' (same role: something used to measure)
distractor 'an anomaly' replaced by 'a rarity' (same role: a departure from the normal)
distractor 'a malfunction' replaced by 'a breakdown' (same role: an equipment fault)
stem reworded to 'Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?'
key word noise kept

passage: In the 1700s, Parliament set each English canal's tolls in a law. The law set a top price and a bottom price. A company could not charge more than the published list, or charge one trader less than another for the same cargo. Some historians say the bottom price was the traders' idea, so no rival got a better deal. But the petitions show the requests for it came from the canal companies, and the traders never mention it. Instead, they asked for lower top prices and complained about every change to the law. A toll stayed where the law put it until Parliament changed it, and Parliament had raised it every time. What the traders feared was ______ tolls.
prompt: Which word best completes the sentence?
key_logic: The traders "asked for lower top prices and complained about every change to the law" because "Parliament had raised it every time," so they feared rising tolls.

distractor_map.role: the historians' reading (traders wanted the bottom price); ruled out because the requests for it came from the canal companies and the traders never mention it
secret prices; ruled out by 'Parliament set each English canal's tolls in a law' and 'the published list'
tolls a company sets as it pleases; ruled out by 'A toll stayed where the law put it until Parliament changed it'

changes: passage cut from 152 to 119 words
'ceiling and a floor' / 'maxima' reworded as 'top price and a bottom price' / 'top prices'
'shareholders wanted an end to rate-cutting between rival canals' cut (the companies' motive is not needed to rule out any option)
distractor 'discretionary' replaced by 'uncontrolled' (same role: tolls a company could set at will)
stem reworded to 'Which word best completes the sentence?'
key word rising kept

passage: Scientists who count moths often use light traps, which pull in the kinds of moths that fly toward bright lamps. _____ many other kinds of moths pay no attention to lamps at all. They can be caught only in traps filled with sweet, sugary bait. So the number of moths counted depends a lot on which kind of trap a scientist picks.
prompt: Which transition best completes the passage?
key_logic: Moths that "pay no attention to lamps at all" are set against the moths that "fly toward bright lamps," so the contrast "On the other hand," fits.

distractor_map.role: treats the lamp-ignoring moths as an example of the lamp-drawn moths
treats the lamp-ignoring moths as more of the same
wrongly makes the lamp-ignoring moths a result of moths being drawn to light

'Entomologists surveying moth populations' simplified to 'Scientists who count moths'
'ultraviolet sources' simplified to 'bright lamps'; 'noctuids and geometrids' to 'many other kinds of moths'
'fermenting sugar' simplified to 'sweet, sugary bait'
'Census totals depend heavily' simplified to 'the number of moths counted depends a lot'
stem reworded to 'Which transition best completes the passage?'
key transition and all distractor transitions kept unchanged; blank kept at the same joint

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions
passage: Long ago, ice houses along the Kennebec River stored big blocks of ice. Workers packed sawdust between the blocks and the walls, because nearby mills had plenty of it. Historian Ora Fenwick found that sawdust from pine trees held water longer than sawdust from hardwood trees. By August, the pine sawdust had turned into a wet, packed crust. _____ ice houses packed with pine lost about one fifth more ice each summer than houses packed with maple shavings.
prompt: Which transition best completes the passage?
key_logic: The pine sawdust that "turned into a wet, packed crust" is the cause and the extra ice loss is its effect, so "As a result," fits.

distractor_map.role: presents the two facts as parallel measurements rather than cause and effect
reverses the direction, offering the loss as a reason to believe the crust claim
denies the cause-and-effect link

changes: passage rewritten at grade 5 (58 words in source; 77 here, split into shorter sentences)
'Nineteenth-century ice houses along the Kennebec' reworded as 'Long ago, ice houses along the Kennebec River stored big blocks of ice'
'mill towns had it in surplus' simplified to 'nearby mills had plenty of it'
'resinous pine held moisture longer than hardwood dust and matted into a damp crust' simplified into two sentences
'roughly a fifth more ice over a season' simplified to 'about one fifth more ice each summer'
stem reworded to 'Which transition best completes the passage?'

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions
passage: In the Middle Ages, stone workers carved their own marks into the blocks they shaped. Recently, historians made a count of these marks at Amiens. It let them follow single workers from one part of the building to another. _____ one mark, a V shape with a bar, appears in the south part of the building and again, forty years later, in the west towers. Historian Piet Vandal thinks this shows one worker's long career, not a mark that someone else used again.
prompt: Which transition best completes the passage?
key_logic: The V-and-bar mark is one case of historians being able to "follow single workers from one part of the building to another," so "For instance," fits.

distractor_map.role: restates the earlier claim instead of giving a case of it
sets up an alternative the sentence does not offer
sets up a replacement the sentence does not offer

changes: passage rewritten at grade 6 (58 words in source; 82 here, split into shorter sentences)
'Medieval masons cut personal marks into the blocks they dressed' simplified
'a recent census of these marks' simplified to 'historians made a count of these marks'
'chevron-and-bar mark' simplified to 'a V shape with a bar'; 'south transept' to 'the south part of the building'
'not a reused sign' turned into 'not a mark that someone else used again'

map_area: Writing: Write, Revise Texts for Purpose and Audience
map_strand: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions
passage: Osier willow is cut in winter, when its thin branches, called rods, are bare and the sap has drawn down into the roots. The fresh rods are tied into bundles and stood in shallow water, where they stay until spring. _____ the basketmaker sorts last season's dried rods by length and thickness. By April, both batches are ready for the workbench.
prompt: Which transition best completes the passage?
key_logic: The sorting happens during the same stretch in which the fresh rods "stay until spring" in the water, and "By April, both batches are ready," so "Meanwhile," fits.

distractor_map.role: marks a concession that the two activities do not involve
marks a summary, but the sentence adds a new activity
marks a replacement, but the two activities run side by side

changes: passage lengthened from 55 to 60 words with a gloss of rods ("its thin branches, called rods")
'bundled' reworded as 'tied into bundles'; 'stock' as 'rods'; 'bench' as 'workbench'

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Sociable weaver birds in the Kalahari build huge shared nests. Dozens of bird pairs live in one nest, and a nest can last for generations. Scientists long believed that every bird gained about the same from living together: warmth and safety. A newer idea disagrees. It says the strongest pairs keep the warm, steady rooms in the center for themselves. They let weaker birds live in the outer rooms only because those birds take the worst of the weather and the attacks, which shields the center. On this view, the nest looks friendly from outside, but it holds together because the weak cannot claim the better rooms.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would best support the newer idea?
choices: Birds in the outer rooms stay warmer on cold nights because of the heat of the whole nest.
Birds in the outer rooms that try to move into the center are chased back by the pairs living there.
Birds in the center rooms are attacked by predators just about as often as birds in the outer rooms.
Nests with many bird pairs raise more chicks in all than nests with only a few bird pairs do.
correct_answer: Birds in the outer rooms that try to move into the center are chased back by the pairs living there.
key_logic: The newer idea says the nest holds together "because the weak cannot claim the better rooms"; outer birds being chased back when they try to move into the center shows that force keeps them out.

distractor_map.adapted: Birds in the outer rooms stay warmer on cold nights because of the heat of the whole nest.
distractor_map.source: Subordinate birds on the periphery gain measurable warmth from the collective mass of the nest during cold desert nights.
distractor_map.role: supports the older shared-benefit view the newer idea rejects

distractor_map.adapted: Birds in the center rooms are attacked by predators just about as often as birds in the outer rooms.
distractor_map.source: Central and peripheral chambers experience nearly identical rates of predation.
distractor_map.role: weakens the newer idea by erasing the shielding advantage

distractor_map.adapted: Nests with many bird pairs raise more chicks in all than nests with only a few bird pairs do.
distractor_map.source: Colonies with more residents fledge more chicks overall than smaller colonies do.
distractor_map.role: true but irrelevant to whether the arrangement is forced or shared

changes: passage cut from 131 to 107 words
'asymmetric coercion' / 'dominant pairs monopolize the thermally stable central chambers' simplified to 'the strongest pairs keep the warm, steady rooms in the center for themselves'
'tolerate subordinates on the exposed periphery' simplified to 'let weaker birds live in the outer rooms'
'Cooperation ... is a byproduct of exploitation rather than its foundation' cut; the closing 'looks communal ... inability of the weak to claim the better rooms' kept, simplified
stem reworded from 'most strengthen the recent model's claim' to 'best support the newer idea'
'periphery'/'peripheral' reworded as 'outer rooms' and 'central chambers' as 'center rooms' in all options
key option says "chased back by the pairs living there" rather than repeating the passage word "strongest" (R7)
same claim and same four findings kept, simplified

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: A psychologist had an idea about memory. She thought people remember facts better when they expect to teach them to others than when they expect only a test. Her reason was that planning to teach makes people sort out the facts more carefully. To test her idea, she wanted proof that the difference comes from the expecting itself. It should not come from actually explaining the facts out loud.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the psychologist's idea?
choices: People who taught a lesson out loud remembered more than people who studied silently for the same time.
People said they enjoyed studying more when they expected to teach than when they expected a test.
People told they would teach remembered more than people told they would get a test, but no one taught.
People tested right after they studied remembered more than people tested a week later, no matter what they were told.
correct_answer: People told they would teach remembered more than people told they would get a test, but no one taught.
key_logic: Better memory from only expecting to teach, when no one actually taught, shows the difference "comes from the expectation itself, not from actually explaining the material out loud."

distractor_map.adapted: People who taught a lesson out loud remembered more than people who studied silently for the same time.
distractor_map.source: Participants who actually delivered a lesson aloud remembered the material better than those who spent the same amount of time studying it silently on their own.
distractor_map.role: shows the effect of actually explaining aloud, the factor she wanted to rule out

distractor_map.adapted: People said they enjoyed studying more when they expected to teach than when they expected a test.
distractor_map.source: Participants reported enjoying study sessions more when they expected to teach the material than when they expected a test on it.
distractor_map.role: about enjoyment, not memory

distractor_map.adapted: People tested right after they studied remembered more than people tested a week later, no matter what they were told.
distractor_map.source: Participants tested immediately after studying recalled more than those tested a week later, whatever they had been told to expect.
distractor_map.role: about timing of the test, unrelated to the expectation

changes: passage reworded from 59 to 69 words, split from 2 long sentences into 5 short ones
'prompts deeper organization of the material' simplified to 'makes people sort out the facts more carefully'; 'information'/'material' reworded as 'facts'

'To isolate this effect, she wanted evidence that the difference arises from the expectation itself' simplified to 'To test her idea, she wanted proof that the difference comes from the expecting itself'
stem 'hypothesis' reworded as 'idea'
options: 'Participants' reworded as 'People'; 'recalled' as 'remembered'; 'even though neither group ever taught it' shortened to 'though no one taught'
same hypothesis and same four findings kept, simplified

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly than countries without them. This pattern, called the "resource curse," is often taken to show that natural wealth harms an economy by itself. Some economists disagree. In their view, sudden resource wealth does not damage a country's institutions, such as its courts and government, if they were sound to begin with. Instead, the wealth tends to arrive in countries whose institutions were already weak. It just makes that weakness easier to see and better funded. Where honest, accountable institutions existed before a discovery, they found, growth did not drop afterward. On this view, the curse is not caused by the resource. It is an older problem that the resource exposes.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the argument in the passage?
choices: In several countries, growth fell sharply in the years right after a big mineral find.
A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.
Countries with strong institutions tend to make and sell more kinds of goods than countries that rely on one export, such as oil.
Sudden resource wealth has been shown to weaken institutions in countries that were well run before a find.
correct_answer: A country with weak institutions before it found oil still grew slowly even after the oil ran out.
key_logic: The economists argue the curse "is not caused by the resource" but is "an older problem"; slow growth that continues after the oil is gone shows the weakness does not depend on the resource.

distractor_map.adapted: In several countries, growth fell sharply in the years right after a big mineral find.
distractor_map.source: In several countries, growth rates fell sharply in the years immediately following a major mineral discovery.
distractor_map.role: restates the raw pattern and fits the 'resource harms by itself' view the passage rejects

distractor_map.adapted: Countries with strong institutions tend to make and sell more kinds of goods than countries that rely on one export, such as oil.
distractor_map.source: Countries with strong institutions tend to have more diversified economies than countries dependent on a single export such as oil or minerals.
distractor_map.role: true but irrelevant to the cause of slow growth

distractor_map.adapted: Sudden resource wealth has been shown to weaken institutions in countries that were well run before a find.
distractor_map.source: Resource windfalls have been shown to weaken the institutions of countries that were well governed before a discovery.
distractor_map.role: contradicts the claim that the wealth does not damage sound institutions, so it would weaken the argument

changes: passage cut from 122 to 120 words
'economically corrosive in itself' simplified to 'harms an economy by itself'
'resource windfalls do not degrade otherwise sound institutions' simplified, with a short gloss of institutions ('such as its courts and government')
closing sentence 'What looks like wealth causing dysfunction is dysfunction determining how wealth is used' cut (repeats the previous sentence)
stem 'the argument advanced in the text' reworded as 'the argument in the passage'

options: 'more diversified economies' reworded as 'make and sell more kinds of goods'; 'windfalls' as 'sudden resource wealth'; 'well governed' as 'well run'; 'depleted and the windfall had ended' as 'ran out'; 'major mineral discovery' as 'big mineral find'; 'a single export such as oil or minerals' as 'one export, such as oil'
same claim and same four findings kept, simplified

map_strand: Analyze Central Idea, Concepts, and Events; Summarize
passage: Many warblers sing long, complicated songs. The usual explanation is that these songs are honest signals. Only strong, healthy males can afford the energy it takes to sing them, so females who choose fancy singers get better mates. Kowalski's field data challenge this idea. Over nine seasons, the chicks of males with the most complex songs were no more likely to survive than the chicks of plain singers. Females paired with fancy singers did not raise more young, either. Kowalski argues that complex song lasts not because it helps choosy females, but because nothing punishes males for producing it. Once the trait appeared, nothing worked against it.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Kowalski's explanation?
choices: Females went to a speaker that played complex songs faster than to one that played simple songs, every time.
Males with complex songs were caught by predators or worn out no more often than males with simple songs.
In a closely related kind of warbler, songs have grown simpler and simpler over the last one hundred years.
Males raised alone developed much simpler songs than young males that heard adult birds singing.
correct_answer: Males with complex songs were caught by predators or worn out no more often than males with simple songs.
key_logic: Kowalski says complex song lasts "because nothing punishes males for producing it"; complex singers being caught or worn out no more often than simple singers is direct evidence that there is no penalty.

distractor_map.adapted: Females went to a speaker that played complex songs faster than to one that played simple songs, every time.
distractor_map.source: Females consistently approached recordings of complex songs more quickly than recordings of simple songs.
distractor_map.role: supports the honest-signal, female-choice view Kowalski argues against

distractor_map.adapted: In a closely related kind of warbler, songs have grown simpler and simpler over the last one hundred years.
distractor_map.source: In a closely related warbler species, average song complexity has declined steadily over the past century.
distractor_map.role: concerns a different species and a decline, not why complexity lasts here

distractor_map.adapted: Males raised alone developed much simpler songs than young males that heard adult birds singing.
distractor_map.source: Males raised in isolation developed markedly simpler songs than males exposed to adult tutors.
distractor_map.role: about how song is learned, unrelated to why complex song is kept

changes: passage cut from 140 to 107 words
'afford the metabolic expense of singing' simplified to 'afford the energy it takes to sing them'
'gained no measurable increase in reproductive success' simplified to 'did not raise more young'
'is not being maintained by the benefits it confers on choosy females but by the simple absence of any penalty' simplified
closing sentence about 'a supposed triumph of adaptive design ... evolutionary accident' cut (not needed to decide any option)
stem 'for the persistence of song complexity' cut; 'Kowalski's explanation' kept

options: 'consistently approached recordings' reworded as 'went to a speaker that played ... every time'; 'elaborate repertoires' reworded as 'complex songs'; 'suffered no higher rates of predation or exhaustion' as 'caught by predators or worn out no more often'; 'in isolation' as 'alone'; 'exposed to adult tutors' as 'heard adult birds sing'
same claim and same four findings kept, simplified
